faq.title: Is Fediverse sharing enabled by default on Threads?
faq.description: No. Meta implemented Fediverse sharing as an opt-in beta feature for public Threads accounts over 18 years old. You must explicitly navigate to Account Settings > Fediverse sharing and toggle it on before your posts federate to Mastodon and other ActivityPub instances.

faq.title: If I delete a post on Threads, does it automatically delete on Mastodon servers?
faq.description: Threads broadcasts an ActivityPub Delete activity to remote Fediverse instances. However, because remote instances are operated by independent third parties, Meta cannot legally or technically force remote servers to honor the deletion. If a remote server has caching bugs or malicious scrapers, copies of your post may persist indefinitely on foreign servers.

faq.title: Can private Threads accounts share to the Fediverse?
faq.description: No. Under the current ActivityPub implementation, only public Threads profiles can enable Fediverse sharing. If you switch your Threads profile from public to private, your existing federated followers on Mastodon will no longer receive your new posts.

html:
When Meta launched Threads in July 2023 as a direct competitor to X (formerly Twitter), it paired its rapid rollout with an unprecedented corporate pledge: Threads would embrace the open, decentralized social web by integrating the W3C ActivityPub protocol. For the first time in the history of Big Tech, a mainstream corporate social platform with hundreds of millions of users was opening its borders to federate with grassroots, open-source instances across the Fediverse (such as Mastodon, Pixelfed, and Lemmy).

This integration marks a massive technical milestone, allowing a Mastodon user on mastodon.social to follow, read, and reply to a Threads creator without ever creating an Instagram or Meta account. However, bridging a centralized trillion-dollar corporate surveillance architecture with a privacy-conscious, decentralized cooperative network introduces profound technical friction: data propagation delays, immutable remote server caching, defederation battles, and complex privacy boundaries. Understanding how Threads federation operates under the hood is vital before flipping the switch.

The Technical Architecture of Meta's ActivityPub Bridge

Meta did not rebuild Threads from scratch as a native ActivityPub daemon. Instead, Threads operates on Meta's ultra-scalable internal infrastructure (derived from Instagram's distributed Django and C++ backends). To interact with the Fediverse, Meta engineered an asynchronous ActivityPub Gateway Proxy:

  1. Actor Mapping: When a Threads user enables Fediverse sharing, Meta's gateway mints an ActivityPub Actor JSON document accessible at: 
    https://www.threads.net/ap/users/@alice
    To the outside Fediverse, Alice's handle appears as @alice@threads.net. Meta signs outbound JSON-LD activities using an RSA-2048 public key advertised in Alice's Actor document.
  2. Outbound Delivery Pipeline: When Alice publishes a post on Threads, internal messaging queues push the post to Meta's outbound federation workers. The workers convert the internal database record into an ActivityPub Create(Note) JSON payload and broadcast it over HTTP POST to the sharedInbox endpoints of remote instances where Alice's federated followers reside.
  3. Inbound Reply Ingestion: When a Mastodon user replies to Alice's post, their server sends a Create(Note) activity to Threads' inbound inbox. Threads' workers verify the remote server's cryptographic HTTP Signature, sanitize the HTML content to strip malicious script injection, and inject the reply into the Threads mobile app UI view hierarchy.

Privacy Boundaries: What Happens When You Opt In?

Fediverse sharing is disabled by default. When you navigate to Settings > Account > Fediverse sharing and toggle it on, your privacy threat model expands across three critical vectors:

  • Loss of Unilateral Data Deletion: On centralized Threads, when you tap "Delete Post", Meta's internal database drops the row from its servers. In the Fediverse, Threads broadcasts an ActivityPub Delete activity. However, because foreign instances are run by independent third parties, Meta has zero technical authority over remote databases! If a rogue server operator runs modified software that ignores Delete payloads, your deleted post remains archived on that server permanently.
  • Public Content Indexing: In the open Fediverse, public posts are routinely crawled by decentralized archival bots, academic researchers, and search engines. Content shared to the Fediverse leaves Meta's protective terms-of-service boundary.
  • Unmoderated Cross-Instance Interactions: While Meta enforces strict automated content moderation within Threads, Mastodon instances operate under independent community guidelines. Users from unmoderated foreign instances can view and reply to your federated posts, requiring you to utilize client-side blocking and muting tools.

The Fediverse Defederation War: The Anti-Meta Pact

The arrival of Threads triggered fierce ideological debate across the Fediverse. Hundreds of independent Mastodon and Lemmy instance administrators signed the Fediverse Anti-Meta Pact, proactively blocking Meta's domain (threads.net) at the server firewall level before federation launched:

Perspective Key Arguments & Architectural Realities
Pro-Federation Instances Embraces open protocols, bridges decentralized communities to 150M+ mainstream users, proves that open standards can defeat corporate walled gardens, accelerates ActivityPub adoption.
Defederating Instances (Block Threads) Fears "Embrace, Extend, Extinguish" corporate monopolization, opposes Meta's ad surveillance model, protects vulnerable marginalized communities from mass algorithmic scraping and corporate astroturfing.

If you federate your Threads account, keep in mind that followers residing on defederated servers (e.g., servers that block threads.net) will simply see an error when trying to resolve your profile.

Step-by-Step: Enabling and Managing Fediverse Sharing

To safely activate Fediverse federation on your Threads profile, follow this workflow:

  1. Ensure your Threads account is set to Public (private accounts cannot federate).
  2. Open the Threads mobile app, navigate to your profile, and tap the settings menu (two lines).
  3. Tap Account and select Fediverse sharing.
  4. Review the informational overview regarding cross-server distribution and tap Next.
  5. Tap Turn on sharing and confirm with your account password.
  6. To verify your handle, open a Mastodon client (e.g., Ivory, Elk, or Mastodon web) and search for: 
    @YOUR_USERNAME@threads.net
    Your profile will appear with your avatar, bio, and published federated posts!

W3C ActivityStreams 2.0 JSON-LD Object Modeling in Threads

To communicate with independent servers, Meta converts its internal relational database records into standardized W3C ActivityStreams 2.0 JSON-LD objects. A production Threads federated post payload includes complex nested metadata structures:

{
  "@context": [
    "https://www.w3.org/ns/activitystreams",
    "https://w3id.org/security/v1"
  ],
  "id": "https://www.threads.net/ap/activities/create-84920412",
  "type": "Create",
  "actor": "https://www.threads.net/ap/users/@alice",
  "published": "2026-11-28T10:00:00Z",
  "to": ["https://www.w3.org/ns/activitystreams#Public"],
  "cc": ["https://www.threads.net/ap/users/@alice/followers"],
  "object": {
    "id": "https://www.threads.net/ap/objects/note-84920412",
    "type": "Note",
    "attributedTo": "https://www.threads.net/ap/users/@alice",
    "content": "
Exploring decentralized federation protocols on Threads!
",
    "url": "https://www.threads.net/@alice/post/84920412",
    "attachment": []
  }
}

Notice the to and cc addressing arrays: because the post is public, it targets the special ActivityStreams #Public URI, signaling to remote Mastodon servers that the post is permitted to appear on the public federated timeline. Outbound HTTP requests are authenticated using Draft Cavage HTTP Signatures, requiring receiving servers to fetch Meta's public key from https://www.threads.net/ap/users/@alice#main-key to verify the payload digest.

Bidirectional Thread Synchronization and Reply Tree Collisions

While publishing a top-level post from Threads to Mastodon is technically straightforward, synchronizing Conversational Reply Trees across distributed systems is notoriously complex:

  • InReplyTo Resolution: When a Mastodon user replies to a federated Threads post, their instance emits an ActivityPub Create(Note) with an inReplyTo field referencing Meta's canonical object URL.
  • Signature and Content Sanitization: Meta's ingress workers verify the remote instance's HTTP signature, strip dangerous HTML attributes (such as <script>, <style>, and onclick event handlers), parse custom Fediverse emojis, and insert the reply into the Threads database.
  • Missing Branch Problem: If Server B replies to a post on Server A, and Server C only follows Server B, Server C's users might see the reply without seeing the original parent post, resulting in disjointed, confusing conversation fragments. Threads mitigates this by aggressively backfilling parent context trees via asynchronous REST queries.

The Future Roadmap: Direct Messages, Polls, and Media Federation

Meta's engineering team has outlined a phased rollout for full ActivityPub feature parity:

  1. Phase 1 (Completed): Unidirectional outbound publishing of public text posts, photos, and links from Threads to the Fediverse.
  2. Phase 2 (Active Rollout): Inbound reply ingestion, allowing Threads creators to read, like, and reply to Mastodon users directly from within the Threads client interface.
  3. Phase 3 (Under Development): Interactive features including poll voting synchronization, custom image alt-text preservation, and content warning (CW) tag translation between Mastodon and Threads.

However, end-to-end encrypted direct messaging and private group federation remain deliberately excluded from Meta's ActivityPub roadmap due to architectural and regulatory complexities.

ActivityPub Cryptographic Key Rotation and Recovery Ceremonies

When operating an ActivityPub actor identity, cryptographic trust is anchored to the actor's public key advertised at their HTTPS ID endpoint. If Meta's signing infrastructure needs to rotate Alice's keypair—or if a user migrates away from Threads to a self-hosted Mastodon or GoToSocial node—a formal Key Rotation Protocol is executed:

  • Signed Update Payloads: Threads generates an Update(Person) activity containing the new public RSA/Ed25519 key, signed with the previous active private key. Remote Fediverse servers verify the cryptographic signature against their cached copy of the old key, ensuring that an attacker cannot arbitrarily hijack an actor by spoofing DNS records.
  • Actor Tombstoning and Dead-Drop Protection: If a user deletes their Threads account, Meta's federation bridge broadcasts a signed Tombstone object, notifying remote instances to purge the actor from search autocomplete indices and cease routing outbound notifications.

Fediverse Content Warning (CW) and Spoiler Tag Interoperability

Mastodon communities rely heavily on Content Warnings (CWs) to collapse sensitive discussions, political debates, and movie spoilers behind clickable summary tags. In early ActivityPub bridges, Threads lacked native CW support, causing collapsed posts to render fully expanded across user feeds.

Modern revisions of the Threads federation bridge translate ActivityStreams summary properties into native expandable warning headers. When a Threads user marks a post with an sensitive content warning, the bridge serializes the warning into the standardized summary field, ensuring respectful, seamless presentation across all federated ActivityPub clients worldwide. This cross-platform standardization allows users from diverse digital communities to curate their reading experience according to personal comfort and content preferences.

To contextualize Meta's federation architecture within the broader decentralized landscape, compare the three leading social networking models:

Architectural Dimension W3C ActivityPub (Mastodon) Meta Threads ActivityPub Bridge Bluesky AT Protocol
Identity Root Server domain (URI) Meta domain (threads.net) Decoupled DID (did:plc/did:web)
Hosting Model Decentralized multi-server Centralized corporate cloud Federated Personal Data Servers (PDS)
Curation Engine Chronological home timeline Algorithmic engagement ranker Composable open feed generators
Account Portability Follower Move activity only No outward follower export Full cryptographic portability
